lessons.title: Kernel modules: lsmod, modinfo, modprobe
lessons.goal:
Learn what a kernel module is, how to list, inspect, load and unload one, and how the kernel finds its dependencies.

Why it matters: drivers (network cards, file systems, firewall features) are usually modules. When hardware or a feature does not work, the first question is "is the module loaded?"

setup.note: Steps with sudo load a harmless module (`dummy`) and change one sysctl value, then restore both. Use a throwaway machine.

steps.title: The kernel can be extended while running
steps.text: A **module** is a piece of kernel code in a `.ko` file that can be loaded and removed at run time, so the kernel does not need every driver built in. Modules for the running kernel live under `/lib/modules/VERSION`.

run.output: arch crypto drivers fs kernel lib mm net sound vmlinux.ctfa

steps.title: lsmod lists loaded modules
steps.text: Columns: name, size in bytes, and a use count followed by the modules that depend on it. `lsmod` simply formats `/proc/modules`.

run.output:
Module                  Size  Used by
ip_set_hash_net        65536  2
xt_statistic           16384  0

steps.title: modinfo describes a module
steps.text: `modinfo` reads the metadata stored inside the `.ko` file: description, license, parameters, and which other modules it needs.

run.output: Dummy netdevice driver which discards all packets sent to it

steps.title: modprobe loads, and removes
steps.text: `modprobe NAME` loads a module and everything it depends on. `modprobe -r NAME` removes it again. Both need root. We load the harmless `dummy` network driver.

run.output:
coresize
holders
initsize
initstate
notes
refcnt
sections
srcversion
taint
uevent

steps.title: Underneath: a system call loads the file
steps.text: `modprobe` reads the file, finds dependencies in `modules.dep`, and asks the kernel to load it with `init_module` (data passed from user space; used when the file is compressed, as here) or `finit_module` (file descriptor). The kernel then relocates the code and runs the module's init function.

run.cmd: sudo strace -f -e trace=init_module,finit_module modprobe dummy 2>&1 | grep -E 'init_module' | sed -E 's/\(.*\)/(...)/' | sed -E 's/^\[pid +[0-9]+\] //'; sudo modprobe -r dummy

steps.under: A module runs in kernel mode with full privileges. A bug can crash the whole system, and a malicious module is a rootkit. That is why Secure Boot can require signed modules, and why `kernel.modules_disabled=1` can lock loading after boot.

quiz.q: Where are the modules of the running kernel stored?
Which command loads a module and its dependencies?
Which system call does modprobe use to hand the module to the kernel?

check.scenario: A new USB network adapter does not show up. Which steps do you take regarding modules?
check.answer: `dmesg | tail` to see whether the kernel detected it and asked for a driver, `lsusb` for the vendor:product IDs, `modinfo` / `modprobe -c | grep ID` to find the matching driver, `modprobe DRIVER` to load it, and check `dmesg` for firmware errors. If the module is missing, install the package with extra modules (on Oracle Linux `kernel-uek-modules-extra`).

lessons.title: sysctl: reading and tuning kernel parameters
lessons.goal:
Learn how to read and change kernel parameters with `sysctl`, make changes permanent, and see that some are per-namespace.

Why it matters: network, memory and process limits (`net.core.somaxconn`, `vm.swappiness`, `fs.file-max`) are tuned this way. A change that is not persisted disappears at reboot.

setup.note: Steps with sudo load a harmless module (`dummy`) and change one sysctl value, then restore both. Use a throwaway machine.

steps.title: Parameters are files in /proc/sys
steps.text: `sysctl NAME` reads the parameter. The dots in the name are slashes in the path: `vm.swappiness` is `/proc/sys/vm/swappiness`.

run.output:
abi
crypto
debug
dev
fs
kernel
net
sunrpc
user
vm

steps.title: Change at run time
steps.text: `sysctl -w NAME=VALUE` (root) writes to the file. The kernel uses the value at once. It is lost at reboot. We remember the old value and restore it.
steps.under: `sysctl` is only a convenience. The kernel registers each parameter in a table (`ctl_table`) with a handler that parses what you write and validates the range. A wrong value returns `Invalid argument`.

steps.title: Make it permanent
steps.text: Put the setting in a file under `/etc/sysctl.d/`. At boot, `systemd-sysctl` applies all files in order. `sysctl -p FILE` applies one file immediately.

steps.title: Some parameters belong to a namespace
steps.text: Network parameters are **per network namespace**. We create a new namespace with `unshare -n`, change `ip_forward` inside it, and look at the host's value afterwards: it did not change. Containers rely on this (module 37).

run.cmd: sudo unshare -n sh -c 'sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=0; sysctl -n net.ipv4.ip_forward'

steps.title: Errors you will see
steps.text: Unknown names and out-of-range values are rejected.

run.output: sysctl: cannot stat /proc/sys/no/such/key: No such file or directory

quiz.q: What is `/proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward` as a sysctl name?

options: Lost at reboot unless saved in /etc/sysctl.d

quiz.q: You set `net.ipv4.ip_forward=0` inside `unshare -n`. What is the host's value afterwards?
quiz.explain: Network sysctls are per network namespace.

quiz.q: Which tool applies all sysctl files at boot?

check.scenario: You raised `net.core.somaxconn` with `sysctl -w` and the problem went away. Two weeks later, after a reboot, it is back. What did you forget?
check.answer: To persist it: put `net.core.somaxconn = 4096` in `/etc/sysctl.d/90-tuning.conf` and apply with `sysctl --system`. Also check that the application itself uses the bigger backlog (it passes its own value to `listen`).

lessons.title: /proc and /sys in depth
lessons.goal:
Learn the most useful files in `/proc` and `/sys`, what they tell you, and which of them you can write to tune the system.

Why it matters: every monitoring tool reads them. When tools disagree or are missing, you can read the source yourself.

setup.note: Steps with sudo load a harmless module (`dummy`) and change one sysctl value, then restore both. Use a throwaway machine.

steps.title: Per-process files
steps.text: `/proc/PID/limits` shows resource limits, `maps` the memory layout, `fd` open files, `environ` the initial environment, `status` the summary.

run.output:
Max processes             22227                22227                processes 
Max open files            524288               524288               files     
Max locked memory         8388608              8388608              bytes

steps.title: System-wide files
steps.text: `/proc/uptime` (seconds up, idle seconds), `/proc/loadavg`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/stat` (CPU counters since boot), `/proc/version`, `/proc/filesystems` (supported file systems), `/proc/devices`.

run.output: ext3 ext4 zonefs btrfs xfs fuseblk vfat

steps.title: /sys: the device model
steps.text: `/sys` is organised by subsystem. `class/` groups devices by type, `block/` has disks, `devices/` is the real tree, `module/` lists loaded modules and their parameters, `kernel/` has kernel features.

steps.title: Disk queue settings live in /sys/block
steps.text: Each disk exposes its request queue: scheduler, read-ahead, whether it is rotational.
steps.under: The block layer registers these attributes in sysfs with `show` and `store` functions. Reading calls `show`, writing calls `store`. `[mq-deadline]` in brackets marks the active scheduler.

steps.title: Write to tune
steps.text: Many `/sys` files accept a write. We write the **same** value back, so nothing changes, to show the mechanism. Changes made this way are lost at reboot; use a udev rule or a tuned profile to persist them.

steps.title: sched_ext and other kernel features show up too
steps.text: Optional kernel features register under `/sys/kernel`. If the directory exists, the kernel was built with it.

run.output: address_bits btf cgroup config cpu_byteorder debug fscaps iommu_groups irq kexec_crash_loaded kexec_crash_size kexec_loa

quiz.q: Which file shows the resource limits of a process?

options: It is the active I/O scheduler
It is the default for new disks only
Is lost at reboot unless configured elsewhere

quiz.q: How do you know the kernel supports sched_ext?

check.scenario: `top` is not installed on a broken server. How do you read the load average and the memory use without it?
check.answer: `cat /proc/loadavg` and `grep -E 'MemTotal|MemAvailable' /proc/meminfo`. For the busiest process, `ls /proc | grep '^[0-9]'` plus reading `/proc/PID/stat`, or `ps`. All monitoring tools read these files.

interview.a: A loadable piece of kernel code (.ko) such as a driver or file system, loaded and unloaded at run time. See [the lesson](#/lesson/13/kernel-modules).
insmod loads exactly one .ko file. modprobe resolves dependencies from modules.dep, honours /etc/modprobe.d, and can remove with -r.

interview.q: How do you load a module at every boot?
interview.a: Create `/etc/modules-load.d/NAME.conf` containing the module name. Module options go in `/etc/modprobe.d/*.conf` (`options NAME key=value`).

interview.q: How do you change a kernel parameter permanently?
interview.a: Put `name = value` in `/etc/sysctl.d/*.conf` and run `sysctl --system`. `sysctl -w` alone is lost at reboot. See [sysctl](#/lesson/13/sysctl-tuning).

interview.q: What is the difference between /proc and /sys?
interview.a: /proc started as process information and became a mix of processes and kernel parameters (/proc/sys). /sys exposes the structured device and driver model, one value per file. See [the lesson](#/lesson/13/proc-sys-depth).

interview.q: Why can't a normal user load modules, and how can modules be restricted further?
interview.a: Modules run with full kernel privilege (CAP_SYS_MODULE). Restrict with Secure Boot / module signature enforcement and `kernel.modules_disabled=1`.

glossary.def: A loadable .ko file that adds code, usually a driver, to the running kernel.
Loads or removes a module together with its dependencies.
The interface to read and write kernel parameters under /proc/sys.
An isolated copy of the network stack, with its own interfaces and sysctls.
The pseudo file system at /sys exposing devices, drivers and kernel features.
The device manager that creates /dev entries and applies rules when devices appear.
